# nish/crypto/p384

ECDSA signature verification over NIST P-384 (secp384r1).

```ts
import {
  P384_POINT_SIZE,
  P384_SCALAR_SIZE,
  P384_SIGNATURE_SIZE,
  p384Verify,
  p384VerifySha384,
} from "nish/crypto/p384";
```

```ts
import { p384Verify, p384VerifySha384 } from "nish/crypto/p384";

// `pub` is a 97-byte key and `sig` a 96-byte `r || s`, a certificate's, say
const signedBy = (pub: u8[], message: u8[], sig: u8[]): boolean =>
  p384VerifySha384(pub, message, sig)
const signedDigest = (pub: u8[], digest: u8[], sig: u8[]): boolean =>
  p384Verify(pub, digest, sig)                          // a digest from any hash
```

<scalar-grid cols="2">

<scalar-card title="p384​Verify" icon="phosphor/regular/function" href="#p384verify">

Whether `sig` (`r || s`) is a valid ECDSA signature of `digest` under the public key `pub` (FIPS 186-4 §6.4.2): `r` and `s` in [1, n), and the x-coordinate of `u1 * G + u2 * Q` equal to `r` mod n, with `w = s^-1`, `u1 = z w` and `u2 = r w`, `z` the digest's leftmost 384 bits.

</scalar-card>

<scalar-card title="p384​Verify​Sha384" icon="phosphor/regular/function" href="#p384verifysha384">

`p384Verify` of the SHA-384 of `msg`: ECDSA with SHA-384 over the whole message.

</scalar-card>

</scalar-grid>

<scalar-callout type="info">

A public key is the uncompressed SEC1 encoding of SEC 1 §2.3.3, 0x04 then X
and Y as 48 big-endian bytes each; a signature is `r` and `s` as 48
big-endian bytes each. DER, which X.509 and TLS wrap a signature in, is not
this module's business. A key or signature of the wrong length, a key that
is not a point on the curve, an `r` or `s` of 0 or n or more, and a sum that
is the identity answer `false`, never a panic. A digest longer than 48 bytes
is truncated to its leftmost 384 bits (SEC 1 §4.1.4, FIPS 186-4 §6.4).

</scalar-callout>

The module only verifies. It holds no private key and no secret
intermediate: every value it computes on is a public key, a signature or a
digest someone sent, so nothing here is a `Secret` and nothing is wiped.

Ported from fiat-crypto (https://github.com/mit-plv/fiat-crypto), fiat-c/src/p384_32.c and fiat-c/src/p384_scalar_32.c. Copyright (c) 2015-2020 the fiat-crypto authors (see the AUTHORS file). Used under the MIT licence; see std/crypto/LICENSE-fiat-crypto-p384.

<scalar-detail title="What is ported and what is not">

The `p384Fiat*` functions are
fiat-crypto's generated, formally verified Montgomery arithmetic on twelve
`u32` limbs with `u64` products — `mul`, `add`, `sub`, `selectznz`,
`nonzero` and `set_one` mod p, and `mul` and `set_one` mod n — statement for
statement, with fiat's variable names, translated the way
`nish/crypto/p256` translates P-256's: C's out-pointers become a `u64`
answer, each of fiat's `addcarryx`, `subborrowx` and `mulx` helpers here
answering its two outputs packed, the first in the low 32 bits and the
second above them, and the caller declaring only the halves fiat goes on to
read; and each function opens with a length guard, so that the literal
indices after it compile with no bounds check. fiat's 64-bit `p384_64.c`
needs a 128-bit product, which Nish has not got, so the 32-bit files are the
ones ported. fiat's `square` is not: a square is a `mul` of an element by
itself, which costs verification a little time and saves this file 2,500
lines. The scalar functions use the field's four helpers, which fiat
generates identically for both. Everything else in this file — the curve,
the encodings, the inversions and ECDSA — is written for this module from
the documents it names.

</scalar-detail>

<scalar-detail title="The curve">

**The curve** is `y^2 = x^3 - 3x + b` over GF(p), p = 2^384 - 2^128 - 2^96
+ 2^32 - 1, with the base point G and its order n from SEC 2 §2.5.1 (FIPS
186-4 §D.1.2.4). Points are projective (X : Y : Z), Z = 0 the identity, and
are added and doubled with the complete formulas of J. Renes, C. Costello and
L. Batina, "Complete addition formulas for prime order elliptic curves"
(EUROCRYPT 2016), Algorithms 4 and 6 for a = -3, as `nish/crypto/p256` uses
them. Complete means no input is exceptional: P + P, P + (-P) and P + O all
come out of the same straight line of field operations, so a crafted key or
signature that steers `u1 G` onto `±u2 Q` gets the right answer, not a
special case.

</scalar-detail>

<scalar-detail title="Public values, so branches are allowed">

Verification computes
`u1 G + u2 Q` by Shamir's trick: one run of 384 doublings from the top bit
down, adding G, Q or G + Q as the bits of `u1` and `u2` say. Those bits, the
exponents p - 2 and n - 2 of the two Fermat inversions, and the range checks
are all public, and the code branches on them. The field and scalar
arithmetic is fiat's, constant time in its operands all the same.

</scalar-detail>

Private names carry the `p384` prefix because a `std/` module's private
functions share the importing program's flat symbol namespace
(`docs/wp26-stdlib.md` §3e).

## Functions

### p384Verify

Whether `sig` (`r || s`) is a valid ECDSA signature of `digest` under the
public key `pub` (FIPS 186-4 §6.4.2): `r` and `s` in [1, n), and the
x-coordinate of `u1 * G + u2 * Q` equal to `r` mod n, with `w = s^-1`,
`u1 = z w` and `u2 = r w`, `z` the digest's leftmost 384 bits. A key or
signature of the wrong length, a key that is not a point on the curve, and
a sum that is the identity all answer `false`.

ECDSA is malleable, and so is this: when `(r, s)` verifies, `(r, n - s)`
verifies too, as FIPS 186-4 and SEC 1 have it. Nothing here asks for the
lower `s`, so a protocol that needs one signature per message and key has to
refuse the upper half itself.

```ts
function p384Verify(
  pub: u8[],
  digest: u8[],
  sig: u8[],
): boolean
```

<scalar-field name="pub" type="u8[]" required>

The signer's 97-byte uncompressed public key.

</scalar-field>

<scalar-field name="digest" type="u8[]" required>

The message's hash; only its leftmost 384 bits count.

</scalar-field>

<scalar-field name="sig" type="u8[]" required>

The 96-byte signature `r || s`.

</scalar-field>

<scalar-field name="returns" type="boolean">

`true` when the signature is valid, `false` for anything else.

</scalar-field>

### p384VerifySha384

`p384Verify` of the SHA-384 of `msg`: ECDSA with SHA-384 over the whole message.

```ts
function p384VerifySha384(
  pub: u8[],
  msg: u8[],
  sig: u8[],
): boolean
```

<scalar-field name="pub" type="u8[]" required>

The signer's 97-byte uncompressed public key.

</scalar-field>

<scalar-field name="msg" type="u8[]" required>

The whole message, hashed here.

</scalar-field>

<scalar-field name="sig" type="u8[]" required>

The 96-byte signature `r || s`.

</scalar-field>

<scalar-field name="returns" type="boolean">

`true` when the signature is valid, `false` for anything else.

</scalar-field>
